town-and-gown-go-to-court-redistricting-.title: Town and Gown Go to Court: Redistricting Fight Hits Boone, NC
town-and-gown-go-to-court-redistricting-.content:
Image Credit: Appalachian State University, https://www.appstate.edu/.

Editor’s Note: This essay was submitted as part of The Politic’s 2026 High School Essay Competition. The author, Andrew Larsen, is a senior at Watauga High School in Boone, North Carolina, USA.

Like many college towns, Boone, North Carolina, has a town-gown divide. Recently, this has spilled into local election politics. Redistricting troubles and accusations of gerrymandering followed a new voting map introduced by the North Carolina Legislature in 2023. Critics contend that dividing Boone and Appalachian State University between two districts splits liberal voters and gives a significant advantage to conservative candidates. Meanwhile, supporters argue that the map provides a greater voice to local rural voters, instead of non-local students. At its heart, it’s a debate about political representation in a community with different claims to belonging. 

Across the country, redistricting has become a focal point of partisan rancor with state-wide battles in California, Texas, and North Carolina, often listed as one of the most gerrymandered states. Fair election advocacy groups have fought to redraw voting districts, with claims of bias against people of color and reduced value of urban votes. 

But grassroots groups also work within specific counties they believe suffer from gerrymandered districts. One county in such a position is Watauga County in Northwestern North Carolina. The county seat, Boone, is a largely liberal center surrounded by a more conservative rural county, making it a microcosm of the larger fights occurring across the country. The divide is even more stark when school is in session as the population jumps from 19,000 to 40,000 with a left-leaning student body. 

The voting map that the North Carolina Legislature introduced in 2023. Photo courtesy of the Watauga County Board of Commissioners.

Following the introduction of new voting districts by the NC state legislature, the largely liberal county commission utilized a state statute that allowed them to redraw the voting maps if there was a significant population difference between the districts. The proposed map would have three district-specific candidates and two at-large candidates for whom the entire county voted. The articulated goal was to ensure that all people throughout the county were represented without favoring one party, while also not splitting precincts across districts. 


The updated map created by the County Commission in 2024, and voted on in that year’s election. Photo Courtesy of Ray Russell.

The November 2024 election ballot included a referendum on whether to adopt this new map, and 71% of the county voted in favor. Yet, the map was not adopted, as the NC State Legislature, led by State Senator Ralph Hise, preemptively passed a bill to prevent the map from going into effect until 2032. The following year, a coalition of citizens and activist organizations known as the Watauga County Voting Rights Task Force sued the Watauga County Board of Elections, with the NC Legislature intervening in the case shortly after. 

Ray Russell on the roof of his office at Ray’s Weather, located in the heart of Boone. Photo Credits: Andrew Larsen.

Ray Russell is a leading plaintiff in Watauga County Voting Rights Task Force v. Watauga County Board of Elections. Russell is a well known community figure for his local weather service, and was one of the county commissioners during the initial 2023 mapping conflict. As someone whose top issues include “fair voting, fair elections, fair districts,” he viewed the legislation as a “blatant partisan stunt.” 

“It was obviously unfair,” said Russell. “It violated every principle of fair maps and fair voting. Our initial goal was to have the districts thrown out for both the school board and the county commission. To include the school board, it had to include claims that they used inappropriate means to divide these districts. Malapportionment is the technical term. The other big thing is banning the implementation of our plan for the county commission until 2032.” 

On April 3, 2026, the District Court ruled that the plaintiff’s malapportionment claims were beyond the reach of the courts, forcing them to remove the claims from their case. With judges against them and long appeal and trial processes, costs have piled up. Currently, Russell is working alongside Common Cause, a non-partisan grassroots organization focused on protecting democracy in small communities, to raise awareness and money for the case. Cathy Williamson, a board member for the group, is part of that effort. 

“The goals for me are getting more balanced and fair courts that aren’t so agenda driven,” said Williamson. “The other part would be to educate everybody who voted the way that we did. You’re just being ignored. I mean, 71% of the voters voted for it, it’s pretty common sense to me. But that doesn’t mean that a court is gonna see it that way. And the will of the voters is being overturned at every angle, every corner.”

But Terry Oldham, a Watauga County citizen, took it upon himself to conduct his own research, giving a presentation to the county commission about a survey he administered to community members. Speaking with 103 people, Oldham found that rather than 71% of voters approving the commission’s map, 97% were now against it in retrospect, and felt that they had been misled by the language in the referendum. 

“I just hope that the people who are pushing this know that ‘we have 71%’ is not true,” said Oldham. “So it wasn’t a representation. I think people were deceived. People were very confused. I just hope that there wasn’t real deception, that it wasn’t on purpose, that it was just put together quickly.” 

Yet, Oldham’s study didn’t follow scientifically recognized polling principles, with significant limitations given the small sample size and no data on voter affiliation. This makes it unclear if voter opinion has actually substantially shifted since the referendum vote. 

The conservative-led team of defendants, including Senator Hise, argue that the commission-created districts are an attempt to retain Democratic control in the county, and give greater weight to Appalachian State student votes in comparison to local votes. Linda Byrd, the Watauga County Republican Party’s chairwoman, and Braxton Eggers, the chairman of the currently conservative-led county commission, did not respond for comment. Senator Hise’s Office declined to comment, citing potential legal concerns. 

However, Jennifer Coffey, Treasurer of the Watauga Republican Party, said, “Natives of Watauga County have been upset that the town, university, etcetera are making decisions for them and this puts the power back in their hands.”

The new voting districts imposed by the state legislature are expected to have significant consequences in the upcoming election, for example, flipping party representation on the school board by increasing the number of Republican members. The stakes are clear: increased student vote representation leads to a blue shift, and their diminished representation leads to a red shift. 

This case echoes similar conservative efforts to weaken student representation throughout the state. At University of North Carolina Greensboro and North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University, the North Carolina Board of Elections removed on-campus student voting sites. 

The outcome of this case is up in the air, but the debate reflects a deep divide in North Carolina over who are the legitimate political stakeholders in a community. As Cathy Williamson said, “This model will travel right across the state.” At stake, then, is more than a configuration of a single district, but also a broader question of how best to represent the voice of the people.

working-in-the-shadows-mumbais-home-base.title: Working in the Shadows: Mumbai’s Home-Based Female Artisans
working-in-the-shadows-mumbais-home-base.content:
Image Credit: Marcel Crozet / ILO, Flickr, https://citizenmatters.in/the-exploits-of-piece-rate-work/.

Editor’s Note: This essay was submitted as part of The Politic’s 2026 High School Essay Competition. The author, Aadya Jain, is a senior at Oberoi International School in Mumbai, Maharashtra, India.

A price tag reveals a boutique garment cost, but remains silent about the hands that crafted it. In Mumbai’s fashion markets, the delicate luxury of hand embroidery, gold-threaded Zardozi or precise Ari is sustained not by modern factories, but by a hidden army of women working from home. Under a dim domestic bulb, these artisans painstakingly stitch together the fabric of India’s textile economy. Yet, as fast-fashion cycles compress margins, this economic pressure travels downward, trapping these invisible craftspeople in the deepest shadows of the supply chain.

In Mumbai, this workforce remains a statistical blind spot. Official datasets treat home-based work as an extension of unpaid domestic chores, causing what Ellina Samantroy terms ‘statistical invisibility.’ This erasure is framed by the World Bank’s finding of a staggering 57 percentage point gender gap in India’s labour force participation. Paired with three local perspectives from independent artisan Supriya, members of Mission Swayam Siddha, and export merchandiser Esther Johnson, the datasets expose the structural realities of this informal supply chain.

The Piece-Rate Trap

In her small Mumbai home, Supriya sits on a floor rug, guiding an Ari needle through taut fabric. She speaks with pride of a family legacy craft, making “an apparel comes to life with embroidery,” keeping handcraft “evergreen.” Specialising in Ari and Maggam needlework, she produces three patchworks in an afternoon. Thus, an elaborate saree needs over two days of bone-aching concentration.

Supriya’s workshop is a microcosm of a vast informal economy. WIEGO reports that India has 41.85 million home-based workers, 45% of whom work in textiles and garments. While the India Brand Equity Foundation (IBEF) notes that textiles employ over 45 million people, home-based artisans, despite sustaining India’s $4.56 billion craft market, remain scattered, isolated, and stripped of bargaining power.

Where the Money Disappears

This isolation leaves workers trapped in a piece-rate structure that systematically denies them standard labour protections. As Esther Johnson explains, “they are usually engaged through multiple contractor layers rather than directly by brands, forcing them to absorb overhead costs like electricity and needles from their own meagre earnings.”

This regulatory silence represents a structural failure of India’s recent labour updates. While the Code on Social Security (2020) consolidated nine laws, a legal critique by Arpita Ranjan and Aman Yadava in the International Journal for Legal Research and Analysis notes that it leaves subcontracted piece-rate homeworkers entirely undefined. As argued in The Wire, until official frameworks properly define home-based workers, their labour will be systematically ignored. This gap is further compounded by what Madhuri Kankipati identifies in India as a structural failure to formalise labour, where tying basic safeguards strictly to platform affiliation leaves the most isolated unorganised workers completely unprotected.

This legal vacuum directly drives the stark gender-based economic exploitation on the ground. Because the law’s silence shields brands from liability, contractors compress piece rates with impunity, resulting in massive wage disparities. National Statistical Office (NSO) data shows a monthly income gap of around $193 between self-employed men and women in million-plus cities, where men earn almost $314 and women nearly $123 a month. In Mumbai, this gap climbs to almost $345. Nationally, WIEGO figures show female home-based workers average barely $0.29 hourly, compared to $0.58 for men and well below the recommended daily minimum of $4.52.

The Order Chain

This wage erosion is structural, moving through a five-tier pipeline: 

Brand → Exporter → Contractor → Agent → Artisan. 

Intermediaries extract a cut at each link. Under strict target-costing models, brands demand low-cost, rapid delivery. Because labour is the only flexible expense, contractors squeeze piece rates to protect their own margins.

The resulting value capture is stark. In nearby Thane, a Citizen Matters report documented women assembling keychains for just Rs. 2.50 (approx. $0.03) per dozen. With retail prices at $0.12 to $0.24 each, middlemen capture over 95% of the value. For Supriya, seasonal festive spikes like Diwali bring welcomed income, but this labour offers no security or protection against the sudden, unpaid lulls that follow.

A Double Shift

Domestic care expectations also come into play. Focus group participants at Mission Swayam Siddha, an NGO in Mumbai’s informal settlements, explained how household chores consume their mornings, leaving only a brief window between 3:00 PM and 6:00 PM for commercial embroidery.

The NSO’s time-use data reflects this double shift since self-employed urban women average 35 working hours weekly compared to 52 for men. This care burden makes factory work inaccessible, leaving home-based piecework as their sole income source. Yet in cooperative spaces like Mission Swayam Siddha, women escape domestic isolation, learning from mentors and weaving solidarity into a shared struggle.

A Craft in Decline

This traditional livelihood is further threatened by automation. The women of Mission Swayam Siddha note that cheap, machine-made garments have eroded younger consumers’ appreciation for detailed handcraft. Johnson confirms that computerised embroidery machines have captured the mass market, relegating handwork to a niche luxury and bridal couture sector.

Even legal protections offer little shield. While India has secured Geographical Indication (GI) tags for techniques like Lucknow Chikankari and Kutch embroidery to convert traditional crafts into globally recognised brands and safeguard cultural heritage, as highlighted in the Press Information Bureau release in 2026, commercial benefits rarely trickle down. A First Resort report highlights this ‘identity-wage paradox’: GI tags legally safeguard heritage, but do nothing to raise wages for isolated workers disconnected from the registered producer groups that capture the GI premium.

What Reform Would Take

Dismantling this invisibility requires supply-chain accountability. To integrate these workers into India’s formal economy, Esther Johnson suggests three practical steps.

First, she recommends establishing a simplified digital registration system linked directly to supply chains, making it feasible to extend basic social security. Second, mandating supply-chain transparency, requiring brands to disclose subcontracting tiers beyond primary factories to expose outsourced homeworking workshops. Third, setting regional piece-rate benchmarks in consultation with artisan groups to prevent underbidding. For brands, Johnson emphasises that these measures are realistic because they build on existing structures, bolstering traceability and supply-chain resilience.

Precedents prove reform is possible. SEWA has spent decades demonstrating how bottom-up organisation challenges exploitation. Indeed, as Al Jazeera reports, on the 30th anniversary of the ILO Home Work Convention (Convention 177), India’s home-based workers are still demanding equal rights with factory employees. SEWA’s milestone achievements prove what collective action can accomplish, as in 1986, the union negotiated minimum wage baselines for garment stitching. In 2014, they launched the physical SEWA Artisan House, a dedicated producer hub enabling female artisans to sell directly to premium markets, bypassing the commission-taking middlemen who historically swallowed their earnings.

Mumbai’s fashion industry continues to rest on the shoulders of unrecorded home-based women. While modern discourses on ethical fashion highlight sustainable fabrics and carbon footprints, they remain silent on the human hands that embroider the luxury on the racks. For artisans like Supriya, working on a floor rug in Mumbai, the reality of the industry is still written in that quiet, precarious space.

between-two-lists-who-gets-counted-after.title: Between Two Lists: Who Gets Counted After Disaster?
between-two-lists-who-gets-counted-after.content:
Image Credit: Luis Acosta / AFP via Getty Images, https://abcnews.com/International/colombia-earthquake-rescue-operations-continue-224-dead/story?id=135571163.

Editor’s Note: This essay was submitted as part of The Politic’s 2026 High School Essay Competition. The author, Martín Ramirez Pachón, is a senior at Colegio San José de las Vegas in Medellín, Antioquia, Colombia.

By the third bend of the San Juan River, the mud had swallowed Amparo López’s sandals to the ankle. She stepped from a narrow wooden canoe and followed a footpath into the trees. At the first house, sheets of corrugated metal sagged over a mattress soaked by rain. Farther uphill, a crack split the wall of a schoolroom where children had been studying days earlier. Plantain stalks lay flattened behind it. López opened the small notebook she carried against her chest and wrote down what remained: a family name, five people, one damaged home, food, roofing sheets. Then she closed it and kept walking. Another bend. Another settlement. Another name. The river carried her toward the next community. Seventy still remained.

At 7:34 a.m. on August 10, a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck near San José del Palmar, Chocó, the strongest recorded in Colombia this century. The quake eventually affected 15 departments and, by August 21, the national government counted 284,185 people affected and 321 dead. Along the San Juan, however, López was helping build a different record. López, a community census coordinator with the Consejo Comunitario General del San Juan (ACADESAN), was helping document losses across the organization’s collective territory, which spans 72 Afro Colombian communities and is home to roughly 15,000 people. 

“People did not come to us speaking in numbers,” López said in an interview. “They said, ‘My roof fell. My children are sleeping next door. The school is cracked. Write us down.’ So that is what we did.”

Writing a family down, however, is not the same as making that family official. Colombia’s National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) directs disaster victims to register through their municipal government in the Registro Único de Damnificados (RUD). Municipal disaster-risk coordinators, not community councils, enter those records into the national platform. The RUD is designed to identify and characterize victims so government agencies can determine the scale of an emergency and generate assistance.

“That distinction matters,” David Valencia, a municipal disaster-risk official in the San Juan basin, said in an interview. “A community can tell us that 40 families were affected, and that is essential information. But the RUD needs households identified individually. We have to verify the information and enter each case. In a place where getting to one community can take hours, that process does not happen at the speed people need.”

That structure also makes the bottleneck local. Under Colombia’s disaster-risk system, mayors are responsible for risk management in their jurisdictions, and municipal coordinators perform the registration that feeds the national database. A community authority may know within hours which houses along a tributary have fallen, but it cannot simply upload that knowledge into the RUD. The information must pass through a municipality that may itself be dealing with damaged offices, blocked routes, power failures, and hundreds or thousands of new cases.

The earthquake exposed the distance between those two systems of knowing. ACADESAN’s August 18 emergency report said the quake had shaken all 72 communities in its territory. Partial municipal reports cited by the organization documented more than 500 homes destroyed in Sipí and Litoral del San Juan and another 1,780 damaged in Nóvita and Istmina. Yet communications were intermittent, rain had cut access further, and some communities still had not reported their losses. ACADESAN mentioned that, eight days after the earthquake, it had received no official support to distribute among its communities.

The problem extended beyond one river. The Defensoría del Pueblo, Colombia’s human-rights ombudsman, identified censuses, registration of affected people, humanitarian assistance, and differential attention to ethnic communities among the unresolved needs it found after the earthquake. By August 16, its monitoring had recorded 77 reports of impacts on Indigenous and Afro Colombian communities, many involving damaged housing and community infrastructure. Mongabay Latam also reported that published national tallies did not disaggregate victims by ethnicity, even as Indigenous and Afro Colombian organizations produced their own counts.

For López, this parallel counting was not born on August 10.

“We have always had to know who is upriver, who moved, who came back, which family is missing, which community cannot travel,” she said. “The earthquake changed what we were counting, not why we count.”

That history matters in the San Juan, where geography and armed conflict have long complicated movement. Mongabay reported that community leaders trying to verify earthquake damage faced scarce fuel, weak connectivity, and restrictions linked to armed groups. These were not abstract obstacles. A list could stop moving because a boat could not. A family could remain outside a municipal count because the person carrying its information had not yet reached the office or signal needed to transmit it.

Valencia rejected the idea that the gap necessarily reflected indifference.

“The state is not waiting for perfect information before responding,” he said. “Aid has moved while the census is still open. But if we want recovery to be fair, we need a record we can defend household by household.”

The government’s response was substantial. By August 21, the Presidency reported that Colombia had received more than 220 tons of international aid and had moved from rescue toward temporary housing, health support, and early reconstruction. Those figures sit uneasily beside ACADESAN’s August 18 statement that it had not yet received official support to distribute. Both can be true: aid can reach a department before it reaches every community inside it.

That is where the two lists become consequential. Community records can move faster because they grow from relationships already embedded in the territory. Official records carry something different: the authority to convert a damaged roof, a displaced family, or an unusable school into a recognized claim on state resources. The weakness is not that one list is accurate and the other is not. Community councils cannot enter their counts directly into the RUD; municipal disaster-risk authorities must formalize the records.

López said ACADESAN had begun sending its information outward while continuing to gather it inward. Valencia said municipal teams were comparing community reports with the cases they could verify and enter. Neither process was finished. The most revealing finding was therefore not a numerical discrepancy, but a procedural one: the people who could identify losses fastest were not the people authorized to formalize them.

Near the end of her route, López reopened her notebook. One family she had recorded days earlier had finally appeared in the municipal system, she said. Others had not.

“I know they are there because I have sat with them,” López said. “The government will know them when the record reaches it.”

Then she turned to the next page. There were still names to add. 

Sources

Primary Reporting

López, Amparo. Community census coordinator, Consejo Comunitario General del San Juan (ACADESAN). Interview with the author. August 20, 2026.

Valencia, David. Municipal disaster risk management coordinator, Municipality of Nóvita, Chocó. Interview with the author. August 19, 2026.
